bible_refs.note: ἐδικαίωθῆμεν διὰ τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ
Ἐγὼ εἰμι ὁ ἐξαλείφων τὰς ἀνομίας σου
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρтон καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ
ποῖον οὖν τὸ νόμον; ἐξεκλείσθη. διὰ νόμου ἐργῶν; οὐχί, ἀλλὰ διὰ νόμου πίστεως
δικαιωθέντες οὖν ἐκ πίστεως εἰρήνην ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ

The quotation of God's promise to raise up a prophet like Moses matches the LXX wording of Deuteronomy 18:18-19 closely, particularly 'I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers' and 'I will put my words in his mouth'.
The phrase 'faith without works is dead' corresponds to James 2:20 and 2:26, where the same Greek idiom appears; the text attributes this to 'one of the holy disciples', likely referring to James.
The reference to Abraham offering Isaac his son upon the altar alludes to the binding of Isaac in Genesis 22, though no direct quotation is used; the participle ἀνενέγκας points to this event.

choices.term: ὑφ' ἁμαρτίαν
choices.english: under sin
choices.why: The preposition ὑπό with accusative ἁμαρτίαν indicates subjection to sin's power, not merely location; standard Pauline usage for moral condition.
rejected: among sin
in the realm of sin

choices.term: ἐδεήθη ἀναγκαίως
choices.english: it was necessary by necessity
choices.why: The cognate accusative ἐδεήθη ἀναγκαίως emphasizes absolute necessity; rendering as 'it was necessary' alone loses the intensifying force.
rejected: it was needed
there was a need

choices.term: οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν
choices.english: not by works of righteousness which we have done
choices.why: The relative clause ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν refers back to ἔργων, specifying works we performed; separating the relative clause distorts the linkage.
rejected: not by works we did in righteousness
not by righteous works we performed

choices.term: κατὰ τὸ πολὺ αὐτοῦ ἔλεος
choices.english: according to the abundance of his mercy
choices.why: The phrase κατὰ τὸ πολὺ is an idiom meaning 'according to the abundance'; αὐτοῦ ἔλεος is genitive of possession, 'his mercy'.
rejected: according to much mercy
by his plenteous mercy

choices.term: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἐξαλείφων τὰς ἀνομίας σου
choices.english: I am the one who wipes out your iniquities
choices.why: The present participle ἐξαλείφων indicates ongoing action; the emphatic ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ affirms identity; 'I will blot out' loses the participial force.
rejected: I will wipe away your iniquities
I am blotting out your iniquities

choices.term: δικαιοῦσα χάρις
choices.english: the justifying grace
choices.why: The participle δικαιοῦσα modifies χάρις as an active attributive; 'grace that justifies' is accurate but 'justifying grace' better captures the nominalized force.
rejected: grace which justifies
justifying favor

choices.term: ὅτι καὶ πάντες ἥμαρτον καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ
choices.english: that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God
choices.why: The aorist ἥμαρτον indicates a completed action (past sinning); present ὑστεροῦνται indicates ongoing state; 'have sinned and fall short' preserves both tenses.
rejected: all sinned and lack glory
everyone has missed God's glory

choices.term: παρώλισθον γὰρ καὶ τῶν ἀγγέλων τινές
choices.english: for we have slipped and even some of the angels
choices.why: The verb παρώλισθον is first person plural aorist indicative 'we slipped'; τινές modifies ἀγγέλ nominative; 'some angels have also slipped' reverses the subject.
rejected: we have stumbled, and some angels too
some angels have fallen as we have

choices.term: ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ
choices.english: to sum up all things in Christ
choices.why: The aorist middle infinitive ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι indicates Christ's action of gathering up; 'to gather all things into Christ' reverses the directional force.
rejected: to gather everything into Christ
to bring all things under Christ's head

choices.term: ἱλαστήριον διὰ πίστεως ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι
choices.english: a propitiation through faith in his blood
choices.why: The term ἱλαστήριον denotes the means of propitiation (mercy seat); διὰ πίστεως specifies the instrument; ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι locates the basis.
rejected: a sacrifice of atonement by faith in his blood
the mercy seat received through faith in blood

choices.term: ἐπεὶ γὰρ πεποίηται τῆς ἁπαντῶν ζωῆς ἀντάλλαγμα τὸ ἴδιον αἷμα
choices.english: since he has made his own blood an exchange for the life of all
choices.why: The perfect πεποίηται indicates a completed action with present results; ἀντάλλαγμα is accusative of result; τῆς ἁπαντῶν ζωῆς genitive of comparison.
rejected: because his blood was given as a ransom for all life
since he exchanged his blood for the lives of all

choices.term: ἐξεκλείσθη
choices.english: it has been excluded
choices.why: The aorist passive ἐξεκλείσθη indicates a completed divine action; perfect would imply ongoing state; present 'is excluded' loses the decisive past action.
rejected: boasting is shut out
there is no room for boasting

choices.term: τὴν παράεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων πεπλουτήκαμεν
choices.english: by the forgiveness of the past sins we have been enriched
choices.why: The perfect πεπλουτήκαμεν indicates we possess the enrichment; παράεσιν is accusative of means; τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων genitive specifying which sins.
rejected: we have gained richness from overlooking former sins
the pardon of past offenses has made us wealthy

choices.term: νόμον καταργοῦμεν διὰ πίστεως
choices.english: Do we then nullify the law by faith?
choices.why: The verb καταργέω in the present active indicative first plural with διὰ + genitive conveys ongoing action; 'nullify' captures the legal-theological force better than 'abolish' in this Pauline context, and 'by faith' preserves the prepositional sense.
rejected: we abolish the law through faith
do we make void the law by faith?

choices.term: Προφήτην... ἀναστήσω... ὥσπερ σε
choices.english: I will raise up for them a prophet like you
choices.why: The future active indicative ἀναστήσω with ὥσπερ σε compares the future prophet to Moses (σε); 'like you' preserves the pronoun and avoids adding 'me' which is not in the text.
rejected: I will raise up a prophet like Moses
I will raise up for them a prophet as you

choices.term: ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος ὃς ἐὰν μὴ ἀκούσῃ
choices.english: Whoever does not heed that prophet
choices.why: The future subjunctive ἀκούσῃ with ἐὰν forms a conditional relative clause; 'whoever does not heed' captures the generality and condition, while 'that prophet' points back to the previously mentioned prophet.
rejected: the man who shall not hear
if anyone does not listen to him

choices.term: πῶς οὖν οὐχ ἱστῶμεν νόμον διὰ τῆς πίστεως
choices.english: How then do we not uphold the law through faith?
choices.why: The present active indicative ἱστῶμεν (from ἱστήμην) with double negation οὐχ...οὐχ implies a positive expectation; 'uphold' better conveys the establishing function of faith in relation to law than 'establish' or 'maintain' in this context.
rejected: how then do we not establish the law by faith
why do we not confirm the law through faith?

choices.term: ὁ μὲν νόμος ἦν ἐν σκιαῖς, πλὴν ὠδίνων ὁρᾶται τῆς ἀληθείας τὴν μόρφωσιν
choices.english: The law was indeed in shadows, but the form of truth is revealed in the pains
choices.why: The imperfect ἦν contrasts with present middle/passive ὁρᾶται; 'revealed in' captures the sense of ὁρᾶται τῆς... τὴν (the form of truth is seen in the pains), avoiding a wooden 'the pains see the form'.
rejected: the law was in shadows, but the pains see the form of truth
the law was in shadows, yet the form of truth is seen in labor pains

choices.term: οὐκ ἀναιρεῖ δὲ τοὺς τύπους ἡ ἀλήθεια, καθίστησι δὲ ἐμφανεστέρους
choices.english: Truth does not abolish the types, but makes them more evident
choices.why: Present active indicative ἀναιρεῖ and καθίστησι with δὲ marking contrast; 'more evident' is the natural sense of the comparative ἐμφανεστέρους, avoiding 'more manifest' which is less idiomatic in English theological prose.
rejected: truth does not do away with the types, but establishes them more clearly
truth does not destroy the figures but renders them clearer

choices.term: Εἰ γὰρ Ἁβραὰμ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη
choices.english: For if Abraham was justified by works
choices.why: The particle γὰρ introduces a reason; imperfect passive ἐδικαιώθη with ἐξ ἔργων is standard Pauline phrasing; 'by works' preserves the prepositional sense.
rejected: since Abraham was justified from works
if Abraham indeed was justified by deeds

choices.term: δίχα τῶν ἔργων τὴν πίστιν εἶναι νεκράν
choices.english: faith without works is dead
choices.why: The preposition δίχα + genitive with accusative-infinitive construction (τὴν πίστιν εἶναι νεκράν) is rendered naturally as 'faith without works is dead' to match the idiom in James 2, which the text echoes.
rejected: faith apart from works is dead
faith separated from works is a dead thing

choices.term: Ἁβραὰμ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη ἀνενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ
choices.english: Abraham our father was not justified by works when he offered up Isaac
choices.why: The aorist participle ἀνενέγκας (from ἀναφαίρω) indicates prior action to the main verb ἐδικαιώθη; 'when he offered up' captures the temporal relation, and 'our father' translates the possessive ἡμῶν naturally.
rejected: Abraham our father was not justified from works, having lifted up Isaac
Abraham our father was not justified by works in offering Isaac

pass_a_gloss:
When then the Greeks were indeed under sin as not having known the creator, but the Jews as guilty of the transgression of the law, it was necessary by necessity for those existing upon the earth of the justifying Christ; we have been justified for not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to the abundance of his mercy; he himself indeed was also long ago saying through the voice of the prophets 'I am the one who wipes out your iniquities, and I will by no means remember them'; the justifying grace overflows equally into all, I say both Jews and Greeks, that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; glory of God then would reasonably be considered, that neither to know nor to have been born to sin; afterward then certainly of the exaltations of the divinity, every created being; for we have slipped and even some of the angels; but it pleased God and Father to sum up all things in Christ the justifying one freely by his grace; for it has been set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood; since he has made his own blood an exchange for the life of all, he has saved those under heaven, and has made the Father in the heavens gracious and favorable toward us; Where then is the boasting? It has been excluded; For who indeed or concerning what will boast, all being in need and having turned aside from the straight way, and no one at all existing who completely does good? Therefore the boasting is excluded, says the boasting, that is, it has been cast out and destroyed, having no place among us; It was excluded how? By the forgiveness of the past sins we have been enriched, being justified by mercy and grace freely in Christ.

Do we therefore abolish the law through faith? The God of all spoke to the wondrous Moses: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him; and the person who does not heed whatever words the prophet speaks in my name, I will require it from him. How then do we not establish the law through faith, approaching the word from him? And the prophet is called Emmanuel because of the human, who as in the order of Moses is a mediator of God and men. And again, the law was in shadows, but the pains of childbirth reveal the form of the truth; truth does not do away with the types, but makes them more evident. For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God. But I think we must suppose that someone said, those who engage in much discussion about the patriarch Abraham should say this: it is said somewhere to one of the holy disciples, that faith without works is dead. But he adds to these: Do you want to know, O empty man, that faith without works is dead? Abraham our father was not justified by works when he offered up Isaac his son upon the altar.
pass_b_english: When the Greeks were under sin because they had not known the creator, and the Jews were guilty as transgressors of the law, it was absolutely necessary that the justifying Christ should come for those living on earth. We have been justified not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to the abundance of his mercy. He himself long ago spoke through the prophets saying, 'I am the one who wipes out your iniquities, and I will by no means remember them.' The justifying grace overflows equally into all—I say both Jews and Greeks—for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.

Glory of God would reasonably be considered as that which neither comes from knowing nor from being born to sin. Afterward, certainly, every created thing is subject to the exaltations of divinity, for we have slipped and even some of the angels have fallen. Yet it pleased God the Father to sum up all things in Christ the justifying one, freely by his grace. He has been set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, since he made his own blood an exchange for the life of all. He has saved those under heaven and has made the Father in the heavens gracious and favorable toward us.

Where then is boasting? It has been excluded. For who indeed, or concerning what, will anyone boast? All are in need and have turned aside from the straight way, and no one at all exists who completely does good. Therefore boasting is excluded—it has been cast out and destroyed, having no place among us. It was excluded by the forgiveness of past sins, by which we have been enriched, being justified by mercy and grace freely in Christ.

Do we then nullify the law by faith? Certainly not! For the God of all spoke to the wondrous Moses, saying: 'I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And whoever does not heed whatever words that prophet speaks in my name, I will require it from him.'

How then do we not uphold the law through faith, as we approach the word that comes from him? And this prophet is called Emmanuel because of his humanity, who, in the order of Moses, serves as a mediator between God and humanity.
Indeed, the law was given in shadows, but the true form of reality is revealed in the travail that brings it forth; truth does not do away with the foreshadowing, but makes it more clearly seen.

For if Abraham had been justified by works, he would have had something to boast about—but not before God. Yet we must consider the claim that those who engage in much discussion about Abraham our forefather should remember what was said to one of the holy disciples: that faith without works is dead.
But he adds to this: 'Do you want to know, O vain person, that faith apart from works is dead?' Abraham our father was not justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac upon the altar.
